Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Can the minister state what the position is with respect to the status of Indians under the Old Age Assistance Act and the Blind Persons Act in the various provinces?

Inquiries of the Ministry Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of National Health and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman was kind enough to give me notice of this question. The position is that in eight of the ten provinces applications are being accepted from Indians for old age assistance and blindness allowances on exactly the same basis as from other provinces. There is no discrimination of any kind. In Alberta and Saskatchewan the provincial legislation and the agreements between the province and the federal government contain no provision for the exclusion of Indian applicants.
I understand, however, that some question has been raised in these two provinces as to the admissibility of Indians to the benefits of their legislation, and that up to the present time no action has been taken by these two provincial authorities to deal with requests for old age assistance or blindness allowances from Indian applicants. I have already written to one of the provinces and I am today writing to the second province with regard to this matter. The position of the federal government is of course that, in the absence of any provision in the provincial law to exclude Indians, they are entitled to the benefits of this legislation on the same basis as any other residents of the province.
With regard to the second part of my hon. friend's question, of course, in the light of custom, I would have to consult with the provinces concerned before tabling any correspondence between the two jurisdictions of government. I will seek their concurrence or their wishes in the matter.

I should like to direct a question to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Fisheries. Will he explain why foreign trawlers are not permitted to enter Nova Scotia ports to secure supplies, as they are in Newfoundland ports?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. Watson MacNaughi (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
The
hon. member for Halifax was kind enough to leave in my office this morning notice of his intention to ask this question. I also received a telephone call from the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. MacLean) on this problem.
Section 10 of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act prohibits, under penalty of forfeiture, the entry of foreign fishing vessels into Canadian ports or territorial waters, unless otherwise permitted by law or by treaty.
We have no treaties with any countries providing for port privileges to foreign fishing vessels on the Atlantic coast. However, under section 3 of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act, as amended by section 9 of the

Statute Law Amendment (Newfoundland) Act, the governor in council is empowered to authorize the issue of licences to-(a) United States fishing vessels enabling them to enter any port on the Atlantic coast of Canada, and (b) any fishing vessels, enabling them to enter any port in the province of Newfoundland for the purpose of:
1.	The purchase of bait, ice, seines, lines and all other supplies, and
2.	The transshipment of catch and the shipping of crews.
Under this section, the governor in council annually issues an order authorizing the licensing of United States fishing vessels to enter Atlantic ports and any fishing vessel to enter the ports of Newfoundland to purchase bait and other supplies.
In the case of the United States vessels, this privilege dates back to 1888 when a reciprocity treaty with the United States was being negotiated. Pending the negotiation of the treaty these privileges were granted to United States fishing vessels as modus vivendi. The treaty was never ratified by the United States but the modus vivendi licences were continued on a yearly basis until this date.
In Newfoundland, foreign vessels, particularly those of Portugal, traditionally came into port for the purchase of bait and other supplies. When the terms of union were being arranged it was part of the agreement that these privileges would be continued and that the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act would be amended accordingly.
May I ask a supplementary question? Will steps be taken by the Department of Fisheries or the department concerned to correct the situation so far as Nova Scotia is concerned?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I think that is a matter of government policy, and if any decision is made thereon, no doubt it will be announced in due course.
May I ask a supplementary question? What is the situation on the Pacific coast?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I understand that on the Pacific coast they have what is known as reciprocal port privileges.

No steps have been taken to set up the authority because it has been deemed advisable to wait for the formal application of the two governments to the international joint commission before appointing the authority.

I can find no other vote in the estimates which has any connection with the St. Lawrence seaway authority. I take it this is the only vote, and that would indicate that there is unlikely to be very much progress made during the present fiscal year with the St. Lawrence seaway plan. I hope I am wrong.
You are.
Perhaps the minister could give us some further information.

The fact that there is no
other vote in these estimates concerning the St. Lawrence seaway is not at all an indication that there is likely to be no progress. On the contrary, I would say that progress has been remarkably good with our neighbours to the south. Following the appointment of the board of engineers, the representatives of the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec met and agreed upon the form of application which should go to the international joint commission.
That is for the power project.

Yes. Later the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself visited the White House at Washington where we were given the assurance by the President of the United States that he would join with us in an application to the international joint commission for the development of power, it being understood of course that Canada would undertake to develop the navigational facilities on its side of the line. That we did undertake by means of an exchange of notes.
Have they been tabled?

I do not know. Then, a group or team composed of legal experts and engineers representing Canada went to Washington, and there discussed with an opposite team the details concerning the United States application to the international joint commission. Those talks have been going on extremely satisfactorily.
Now, there are still some difficult points to iron out, and the committees are negotiating with each other. I am unable to say when it will be possible to file the application with the commission, but I trust it will be soon.
The application to which the minister refers is an application for permission to instal a power project as distinct from the seaway, is it not?
That is right.
What progress has been made with regard to the seaway?

With regard to the seaway, a large part of the work was in part completed under the original plans, and meanwhile the officers of the Department of Transport, the special projects branch under Mr. Guy Lindsay, are proceeding with plans for the completion of the canal. There have been a number of sites considered for the location of the canal. Borings have been practically completed, or they have been started if they are not completed, to determine the nature of the soil in the vicinity of the area where locks will be constructed. If the international joint commission were, for instance, to decide tomorrow in favour of the joint power project, our plans are in such shape that they could be completed in a fairly short period of time to allow us to go ahead with the navigational features.
But I would remind the hon. member that the navigational features could not be completed or begun, for that matter, until the main dam at the Long Sault, the control dam at Iroquois and the power houses at Maple Grove were completed.
Is it the intention of the government to wait for some further time in the hope that the United States government will agree to the joint seaway scheme?

I do not know that I can answer that except in this manner. We are negotiating with the United States now in the hope that it will be possible to iron out the details of the joint application to the international joint commission for the power project.
There is no intention of Canada going it alone with regard to the seaway at the present time?

Oh, yes, that is what I have been saying all along. I hope I have not left any other impression. That is the object of launching the j oint application with the United States to the international joint commission, that is for the development of power. We have given the assurance that if that is approved by the international joint commission we will proceed with the navigational features.
In what vote do we find the expenditures for these borings? They could not be in this vote?

Yes, in this vote, in which there is a $45,000 increase, and that provides for the expenditures of the joint board of engineers. There is no other vote providing for additional expenditures for plans for the navigational features to which I referred. The supplementary estimates will be tabled later, and if progress is such as to warrant a vote in those estimates we will have that done.

I bring that up because these borings and other preliminary work to which the minister referred cannot be very extensive if the whole of that expenditure, as well as the expenditures of this board, are covered in the $60,000 item which we are now considering.

I would remind the hon. member that most of the personnel are permanent employees of the government and are being paid under other votes. This covers telegrams, telephones, office expenditures, and so on to some extent.

Item agreed to.
Marine services-
468.	Marine services administration, including agencies, $571,414.

I should like to ask the
minister how many steamers are operating in this service in the maritime provinces. I should like to ask also whether the coast guard service comes under this item or items 469 or 470.
May I answer those two questions under the next vote?
Is this not the branch of the minister's department which has charge of the search and rescue work?

No, the Minister of Transport is no longer responsible for this work. It has been transferred to the Department of National Defence, R.C.A.F., search and rescue branch. It was assigned to them following an investigation made by a committee on which the Canadian maritime commission was represented and which was then under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice Clyne, and the recommendation, which was adopted by the government, was that the service would be better looked after by the R.C.A.F.

The Department of Transport has some responsibility, because on page 9 of the last annual report of the department it is stated that departmental vessels, both large and small, form part of a fleet of some 200 government operated ships which have been co-ordinated into a general marine 55704-158
Supply-Transport
search and rescue system in Canada, and which co-operate with the R.C.A.F. and civilian aerial search work. What we would like to know is what part the Department of Transport plays in that work.

The Department of Transport plays the same part as any other departments that own or operate ships. The initiation of search and rescue operations lies with the R.C.A.F. They call upon the various ships of government departments, as they call upon us, and we would go to the assistance of a distressed vessel if our ship happened to be close to the scene at the time; that is the extent of the responsibility of the Department of Transport.

For example, in January of this year there was a plane crash just off the airstrip at Sandspit. Most of the occupants of the plane lost their lives. Some were rescued by a small boat which put out from the shore. The accident occurred within a comparatively short distance of the shore, and there was severe criticism of the government owing to the fact there was no crash boat at that airstrip. That, of course, would seem to be the responsibility of the Department of Transport. I am wondering whether steps have been taken since that accident to have some lifesaving service established, because the airstrip is in a position where an accident of this kind might easily occur and it is used quite frequently. This was a tragic disaster, and those lives might have been saved had there been a crash boat there.

I do not know whether or not I made myself clear a moment ago. To what I said perhaps I should have added this. There are across Canada places where the Royal Canadian Air Force maintains certain air rescue operation centres. From those centres it works by radio, by telegraph, and by telephone the moment it is advised of a casualty. I know something of the disaster to which my hon. friend refers because it was brought to my attention by the air services branch of the department. It was unfortunate that at the time there was no vessel that could go to the rescue of this plane immediately. Notwithstanding that, I think the air force had planes in the air to see what could be done to assist those who were in danger. The recommendation of the committee, however, was that the R.C.A.F. would co-ordinate the services of all departments. We try to serve at their direction.
The hon. member will recall that we discussed coastguard services at some length, but we felt that this perhaps would be the better of the two alternatives, having

Supply-Transport
regard to the cost of maintaining and building cutters. It is true that it does not work out well in all circumstances; but I can refer to other cases in which it has been exceedingly helpful to have our ships in the vicinity of an accident. One never knows when or where an accident is going to strike. We do our best to meet the situation.

Has a crash boat been placed at Sandspit airport since the accident? In this particular accident these people got out of the plane. They apparently got out of the cabin of the airplane and then it gradually sank. Eventually nearly all of them lost their lives. The only ones who were rescued were picked up by some ordinary rowboat or some sort of home-made affair which happened to be available on the shore. I would hope that by this time some lifeboat has been placed there. Perhaps the minister could tell us what the situation is. He knows the place in question is on the Queen Charlotte islands in an isolated spot. If a lifeboat has not been put there since, I hope it will be possible to have one put there without much further delay.
May I ask my hon. friend to await the answer to that question until the air service officers are here? I am not able to say of my own knowledge.

Item agreed to.
Marine services-
469.	Marine service steamers-administration, $63,435.
The minister was going to answer my question on item 469.

The hon. member was
anxious to get a list of our ships in the maritime provinces. Is the Sea

Item agreed to.
Marine service steamers-
470.	Operation, maintenance and repairs, $4,670,783.

I think this is the right item under which to raise a question I am anxious

to speak about, namely the damage to one of the weather ships which occurred during the winter storms last year on the Pacific. One of the vessels was damaged, and I believe it has been partially repaired. The point I want to make is that the crews of these vessels suffer a great deal of hardship owing to the exposed nature of their work. The station is in the middle of the Pacific, in difficult climatic conditions. During the storm I understand that the crew of the vessel had an exceedingly trying experience. It has been suggested that better accommodation could be provided on the ship itself. I know of the good work which the crews of these ships are doing. They are rendering a valuable service. All sorts of agencies rely upon the weather report. I also know, however, of the unpleasant nature of their task, in that they are stationed in the middle of the ocean and are obliged to put up with very inclement weather. I would ask whether any consideration is being given to the matter of whether it is possible to improve the living quarters and general facilities on these weather ships whose crews endure great hardship during winter storms.
I agree with my hon. friend that the life of those who have to stay for long periods of the year on lightships is sometimes a monotonous one. I visited a lightship at the mouth of the Saguenay-
I was referring to weather ships.

I know that; but the lightship at the mouth of the Saguenay gives to the layman some idea of the life of people who are stationed on such ships. My hon. friend referred to a lightship on the west coast.
I was speaking about weather ships.
Out in the middle of the Pacific.
One of those ships that the minister inspected about two years ago, as he will recall, when it was moved.

The position of the crew has been substantially bettered by the vote which we had in the estimates last year and part of which I believe is in this estimate. That is the one which provides for an alternate ship, the St. Stephen, which will be based at Victoria. It will be a sort of stand-by ship and will enable those who are out some 500 miles northwest of Victoria, in the other two weather ships, to be relieved from time to time. Provision has been made for recreational facilities, and living conditions for the men are being considered from time to time by the

superintendent of marine services. I know it is a rather monotonous life; in fact, it is a monotonous life. We try to make it as interesting as possible and as I said before we have now provided three ships to operate the weather station.

It is not so much the monotony of the life to which I refer. I believe that the conditions are almost hazardous during the winter storms. If the minister will look into the matter and see whether something cannot be done to improve the actual conditions of the crew while they are on stations, I should be glad. I know that everything possible is done when they come back into port. But while they are actually on stations 1 suggest that, from the information I have received, improvements can be brought about in their condition. I hope the minister will look into the matter.
I shall be glad to look into it.
At page 521, in the details of services there is an item, "charter of aircraft for aerial ice survey, $15,000". Can the minister tell me what those aircraft are used for and where they are based?

Those aircraft are for the survey of ice in the Atlantic. The object of these surveys is to ascertain what the ice conditions are so that our people can have some idea of when navigation is likely to open.
Where are those aircraft based?
They are based at Charlottetown.

Item agreed to.
471.	Construction or acquisition of vessels and equipment, as detailed in the estimates-capital, $4,351,000.
In this vote there is an increase of nearly $2 million. It has been practically doubled since last year. Can the minister explain why that was necessary?

Yes. This is due exclusively to a program of new ships. I dealt with it in my original statement, but briefly it is due to an item of $3,770,000 which is entirely new, which we expect to spend this year on the ice breaker which is now under construction at the Davie shipbuilding yard at Lauzon. It is also due to an item of $300,000 for a lighthouse supply and buoy vessel for the Saint John, New Brunswick, agency, which will cost $2,200,000. We do not think it will be possible to spend more than that amount on the Saint John vessel this year, 55704-I58J
Supply-Transport
that is, more than $300,000. Then there is for construction and acquisition of equipment for repairs to the Lady Laurier and -certain installations the sum of $246,000, which totals up to $4,351,000.
The equipment item on page 521 of $246,000 is just about ten times the amount voted last year. Why should there be that increase for equipment?

Well, it is not an increase in equipment so much as it is for repairs. For instance, for the reconditioning and fitting of the Lady Laurier, there is $150,000. That is more than an ordinary item, because the Lady Laurier is in pretty bad shape, which my hon. friend would know if he had seen it. She is an old ship, and will have to be replaced in due course, but we feel that if we spend this amount upon her it will keep her in operation for some time.

I notice there have been a great many lightkeepers let out, or they may have been transferred to some other work. Can the minister explain why that was done, and also what disposition was made of these men?

Most of the men who have been let out were assistants to the head lightkeepers who are civil servants. They were under contract and not really civil servants or employees in the strict sense of the word. They were contractors. Some positions have been re-established, but others have been dropped.

Item agreed to.
Aids to navigation-
473.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $1,439,210.

On aids to navigation, when speaking the other evening I drew the attention of the minister -and I wrote to him last year-to the entrance -into Flower's -Cove, where there are posts sticking up, one on an island and one on the land, a very primitive arrangement for entering into a harbour. Has anything been done to improve that situation since?

I have a memorandum covering my hon. friend's point, which he raised

Supply-Transport
earlier, but unfortunately I cannot lay my hands on it. Perhaps I can give it to him a little later on.

When I wrote to the department I got an answer back saying that nothing could be done to it during the current year-that is last year. It seems to me that the expenditure will not be very heavy, and it might be the means of saving a ship some day. That is a very bad port, with a lot of shoals around, and the captain has to be very careful going in. He cannot go right inside. There are just two poles sticking up at the present time, and not very high. He _ asked me particularly to draw the attention of the minister to this matter, and I hope he will give it consideration.
I think I have it now. Representations were made on behalf of the master of the Northern Ranger that range lights be established at Flower's Cove to mark the anchorage.
That is right.

The captain of the ship discussed the matter with the agent at St. John's, Newfoundland. He pointed out that the light maintained at Capstan Point would be much more useful if moved to Harbour Rock. That is being done. He also recommended that in addition range lights should be established, and that is being considered for next year.

I made representation last year to the department about navigation lights going into Bay Roberts harbour. I understand it is to be carried out this year. I do not know whether that has been done yet or not.

I am not able to tell my hon. friend whether it is in this year's estimates or not, but I can assure him, in view of his representations, it will be carefully considered, and if it is not in these estimates perhaps consideration can be given to putting it into the supplementaries.
It is only a small item. I think the cost would be in the vicinity of $1,000. A great deal of shipping goes in and out of there all the time, and it is vitally necessary for navigation.

I do not want to hold up the committee, but I should like to express a word of appreciation of the consideration that the officers of the department who deal with these matters of aids to navigation give to the representations that are made by the fishermen and others who depend on these aids. The officers do not always agree with the requests that are made, but it has been

my experience that they always give them very fair and considered attention, and that certainly in most cases, even if they cannot meet the requests in full, they find some acceptable compromise that meets the situation.
There is one phase of the matter that I think could be given some consideration, and that is the maintenance contracts for spar buoys and other small aids to navigation. These services are carried out by the people of the areas concerned under arrangements made by the department. I think in most cases the amounts paid under present conditions are not sufficiently high. The individuals supply their own materials and there have been increases in cost of paint and that sort of thing. I know that the minister and the department have been giving attention to this matter, but I would urge that the whole matter be given careful consideration to see whether some slightly higher scale could be brought into effect for this year.
The minister did not explain why it was necessary to increase item 473. It is more than double.
Well, I explained that it was because of the new program for ships.
Item 473 is different.
The large project of the ice breaker for the Department of Transport.
That is not item 473.
The details are given on page 524 of the estimates.

It reads:
Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment.
Details are found at the bottom of page 524.

There is a substantial
increase there, due to the construction of a pier and tower at Gross Cap reef on lake Superior, twelve miles above Sault Ste. Marie, at a cost of $350,000, and the Agency wharf at Halifax is being rehabilitated at a cost of $180,000, and work is being done at Quebec at a cost of $70,000. That makes up the total of the increase.
Where is the one on lake Superior?
Twelve miles west of Sault Ste. Marie.

Item agreed to.
Nautical services-
474.	Administration, $158,952.

I believe the training of merchant seamen comes under this item. What plans are now in effect for the training of

young merchant seamen? Is there still any rehabilitation of merchant seamen who served in the last war?
We are contributing certain sums of money to the training of merchant seamen at Vancouver, Halifax, Yarmouth, Saint John, New Brunswick, and in addition St. John's, Newfoundland.

On what basis is that done? Does the department contribute to a vocational training school, does it operate a training school of its own-or just what is the program? How many young men are being trained in this work?
We pay 50 per cent of the cost of operation of the schools. I am informed the provinces operate the schools. I have not the numbers available.
Could the minister get that information?
I can, and I shall send it to the hon. member in writing. We will have to get the information from the provinces.
Is the scheme sufficiently broad to ensure a steady stream of young men qualifying for service in the merchant navy?

I am informed that it is. I have in mind one school I visited last summer. It appeared to be up to date. They have a number of students whom they train to serve as able-bodied seamen, engineers and for other divisions of the merchant navy, including masters, mates and the like. We make a contribution to the operation of the schools. Sometimes we help in the provision of equipment. I was informed by the director of the school I visited that there are more than enough young men going through there to provide for the demands of that district.
Which district was that?

That was Quebec. I visited the school in Vancouver three years ago, and I believe it is one of the most up to date in Canada. It is operated on the basis of a contribution from the federal government. While I do not know of the exact position in Vancouver, I believe I would know if a satisfactory number of merchant seamen was not being provided, because the shipping companies would call upon us for assistance.
Are there still some veterans of the recent war taking training?
I am informed there are still a small number.
Is the scheme being closed off?

Yes.
Supply-Transport
I had intended to ask what was being done in Newfoundland, but I thought that would come under the next vote.
It would; but I did not wish to interrupt the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.

Operation and maintenance, including grants and contributions, as detailed in the estimates; rewards for saving life from vessels in distress; subsidies to salvage companies, and the payment of expenses, including excepted expenses, incurred in respect of Canadian distressed seamen as defined in section 296 of the Canada Shipping Act, $318,364.

I do not
see any amount here for Newfoundland. Is there one? I see one for Vancouver and another for Kingston.
I am informed there is no vote here for Newfoundland. Negotiations are being concluded with the provincial government for the establishment of such a school. That is why it is not here.
I should like to know the details. Is it just by correspondence?
No.
What does the minister mean when he says that arrangements have been made?

I was saying, in effect, that negotiations had been entered into with the provincial government, and my understanding is that they have been concluded. I do not know what the terms of the arrangement are. I would presume however that they would be the same as in the other provinces, namely that Newfoundland would establish a school, maintain and operate it, and we would make a contribution to the extent of 50 per cent.

Let me
advise the minister that we have had a school down there for many years, one which was operated by the Dominion of Newfoundland, when it was a dominion. We had a much higher standing than exists in other schools of navigation in Canada. Our masters had tickets from the board of trade in London, and those tickets are rated higher than the Canadian ticket. Does the minister expect there will be a vote for Newfoundland in this connection in the supplementary estimates this year? Does he expect negotiations will be concluded in time for that?

I cannot say at the moment; but if they are concluded I can assure my hon. friend that there will be an item in the supplementary estimates.

Supply-Transport
The school down there has been operating for a number of years and has been doing remarkable work. It would be useful if encouragement were given.
In item 475 there is reference to rewards for saving life from vessels in distress. Did I understand the minister to say that the Atlantic coastguard service does not come under his jurisdiction.
That is right.

I believe the matter about which I shall now speak would come under the minister's jurisdiction. Last winter, it will be recalled, the Winnie Anne was lost off the coast of Nova Scotia on January 28. The gallant crew of the Gladys E. Sweeney, under Captain Ernest Wilson, went to the rescue of the Winnie Anne, when none of the coastguard boats would venture out. Captain Wilson and his crew, in one of the worst storms ever known on the Atlantic coast, had no difficulty in getting a crew and manning the Gladys E. Sweeney. At the risk of their own lives they snatched from the jaws of death the captain and crew of the Winnie Anne. Had they had proper gear, such as the coastal service should have, they could have saved the Winnie Anne. What is going to be done for the captain and his men?

I shall be glad to look into the case which my hon. friend has brought to the attention of the committee. I remember having seen something in the press about it, but I am not familiar with the details. I shall be glad to look into it and perhaps I can tell him later what provisions if any can be made to cover this case.
I notice that there is a decrease in this item -and I hope that does not mean a lessening of the services with respect to the protection of our seamen.
The decrease is brought about by the dropping of eight positions. These positions have been abolished because schools have been established and it is not necessary to carry these instructors.
There will be no lessening of the service?
It will not affect the service at all.
There is an item in the details of $13,200 for professional and special services; what does that cover?
That is for the payment of legal fees, assessors' fees and court reporters' fees in connection with investigations held under the Canada Shipping Act.
Would the minister satisfy my curiosity about the meaning of the phrase "and the payment of expenses, including excepted expenses, incurred in respect of Canadian distressed seamen."

Section 296, subsection 5, of the Canada Shipping Act reads:
(5) For the purpose of this section, excepted expenses are expenses incurred in cases where the certificate of the proper authority obtained on leaving a seaman behind states, or the minister is otherwise satisfied, that the cause of the seaman left behind is desertion, or disappearance, or imprisonment for misconduct, or discharge from his ship by a naval court on the ground of misconduct, and expenses incurred on account of the return to a proper return port of a distressed seaman who has been discharged at the port at which he was shipped, or at some neighbouring port.

A seaman who belongs to Vancouver may be stranded in London and be shipped back to Halifax and still be as far away from home as ever, since he would have approximately 4,000 miles still to go. We have had people ask for donations to help someone who belongs to Vancouver but who has been landed in Halifax. Would not repatriation in this case mean repatriation to the seaman's home port rather than landing a man who belong to Vancouver at Halifax or a man who belongs to Halifax at Vancouver? If the department assumes responsibility under the act to repatriate a seaman from some other part of the world, should it not also be responsible to see that he gets back to his home port?

I am informed that it would be covered by the articles of agreement. If he signed articles at Vancouver, he would be repatriated there if he did not come under the exceptions in section 296. Otherwise he would be repatriated to the port where he had been taken on.

Are there regulations under that section? A master might declare a man to be a deserter when he was not a deserter in fact. A master might dislike a seaman, put him ashore and say that he was a deserter, and log him as a deserter.
I am informed that there are no regulations, that the matter is governed exclusively by the Canada Shipping Act.
How much money was spent last year out of this vote?
It is not broken down in such a way that I could tell my hon. friend, but I will find out and give it to him later.

Item agreed to.
476.	Pilotage service, including authority for temporary recoverable advances not exceeding $20,000, $421,264.
Has the department considered providing a small tug in connection with the pilotage service at Charlottetown, or is this service to be conducted under the same old system?

This vote provides for pilotage service and other assistance to pilotage districts in Montreal, Halifax, Saint John, Sydney, Quebec and Vancouver. Item agreed to.
477.	Steamship inspection and the carrying out of the provisions of the conventions for the safety of life at sea and load lines, $543,764.

I notice on page 10 of the report of the department for 1951 reference is made to the board of steamship inspection, and this statement is made:
Similarly, meetings have been held with a view of applying the provisions of the regulations to sealing vessels and other ships used in Newfoundland.
The minister may remember that the other evening I referred to fears that are current in Newfoundland that sealing vessels are going to be put out of business through the strict enforcement of the regulations. Has the minister anything to say on that point?

The new steamship regulations will apply also to Newfoundland. I am informed that our steamship inspectors have been in negotiation with the operators of small vessels in Newfoundland and our understanding is that they are perfectly satisfied with the method we are going to adopt in bringing these regulations into effect.
I note that there is an increase in this item of $82,356. Can the minister explain this increase?

The increase in rates of pay announced in December, 1951, amount to $31,000; $68,817 is for 67 annual increases; $33,768 is the additional cost of eight added positions of ship inspectors. My hon. friend will remember that representations were made for additional ship inspectors during the last discussion of the estimates of the Department of Transport. These are the inspectors who will be required and provision is made for them. Not all of the eight have been employed yet but that is the estimate that we expect that we will have to pay. Basic salary rate increases for specific classes due to changes in classification of ship inspectors amount to $3,670, and there is a decrease of $899 for other net salary decreases which brings about the total increase to be found in the estimates.
Supply-Transport
Were these additional inspectors required because of the new fire regulations which resulted from the Noronic disaster?
In part, and also for other reasons.
What is the position now with regard to the enforcement of these new fire regulations?

I would have to take some time to deal with that fully, but to respond briefly to my hon. friend, we have put into effect all the recommendations of the Kellock commission which followed the Noronic disaster, and we have put into effect some of -the recommendations of the Choquette investigation following the disaster involving one of the Canada Steamship Lines ships in the province of Quebec some time ago. As the house will remember, these recommendations were fairly stringent. They imposed the responsibility on ship owners of spending considerable sums of money in order to instal sprinkler systems, fireproof bulkheads, and fire alarm systems. All the operators on the west coast, the great lakes and the St. Lawrence and on the east coast have complied with the regulations.
How often are inspections made of these ships with respect to fire protection facilities? Are they made periodically each year?
They are made or should be made practically every time a ship comes into port.

In Newfoundland we have what is known as the Lloydi's surveyor. When a ship is damaged he examines it to see if it is seaworthy for insurance purposes. Would his inspection be accepted by the inspectors operating under our regulations?

Our ship inspector will accept the survey of the Lloyd's surveyor because that firm is recognized throughout the world. There is another firm whose survey or recommendations our inspector accepts, but the name escapes me at the moment.
Will Lloyd's accept our inspection? We have inspectors to inspect ships. Would Lloyd's have to survey them or would they accept our inspection?
I understand they accept our inspection.
Have you an inspector in St. John's?
We have.

Then there is no need for a Lloyd's surveyor there now. I take it you have taken over the position.

Supply-Transport
The point is some ships are registered with Lloyd's and other ships are not. We send our own inspector to inspect them.
Do you know who your inspector is there?
I am afraid I will have to get the name for you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Item 479 is one where there is a decrease. I note that the decrease of $440,000 odd has been achieved despite the fact that there is an increase of $5,200 for increases in rates of pay, with which I agree. Would the minister indicate the basis of this commendable accomplishment? Does it set a pattern that he might have followed in connection with other items?

Perhaps I might take this opportunity to congratulate the new deputy chairman who has just taken the chair. I take pleasure in doing so not only because he is an able colleague in the house but because he was also a classmate of mine at Osgoode Hall. Nothing pleases me more than to see him occupy this position. I know how successful he was as a student in those days, and I am sure he will preside over our deliberations with fairness and with equal success. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was inquiring as to the reason for the decrease. In the last supplementary estimates we included an amount of approximately $500,000 for maintenance dredging. It was not found necessary to include that item this time, and that accounts for the decrease.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Was that sum of money expended last time?
Yes, it was.

Would the minister give the committee some more detailed information concerning the votes for the St. Lawrence ship channel? Referring to the annual report of the department, I find that the ship channel is 200 miles long and extends from Montreal to below the island of Orleans. I note that it has a depth of 35 feet. I do not know what moneys are voted by the Department of Transport for this channel and what moneys are voted by the Department of Public Works, but perhaps the minister could give us the over-all picture of the situation. Apparently items 479, 480 and 481 all deal with the St. Lawrence ship channel.

Vote 479 is for the administration of the ship channel. Some years ago

a branch was set up within the Department of Transport to deal with the maintenance of the ship channel. The channel is now dredged from a point thirty miles below Quebec city to the harbour of Montreal to an approximate depth of 35 feet. It is not fully that but it is almost 35 feet. Various committees have recommended improvement of the channel from time to time. It was not nearly as deep or wide five, ten or fifteen years ago as it is now. Provision has been made for that. That is taken care of in another vote, but this vote is for the purpose of administration expenses, including salaries of the headquarters organization. There are eighteen members of the technical, engineering and office staffs. Connected with the operation of the ship channel is the operation and maintenance of four inspection survey vessels, including the Ernest Lapointe, for a period of seven months of the year, also three sounding scows and two stone lifters, with a total of 104 full-time and seasonal crew members. Then for maintenance dredging under contract there is the sum of $400,000. Then there is maintenance of beacons and gauges for the ship channel, and expenses of dredging inspectors on the contractor's dredging equipment for which there is the sum of $12,200 odd. That first vote, number 479, deals with the administration of the ship channel.
The next vote is a contract capital vote, and by that I mean that a contract is given by the Department of Transport to widen the channel and build anchorages. For instance, after a Department of Transport committee had for some months given consideration as to whether or not the channel should be widened, additional anchorages provided and the channel deepened in certain areas, it was recommended to the department that a contract involving a certain list of work which is mentioned in the next vote be let. I referred to that in my opening remarks on the discussion of my estimates. This contract has since been awarded to Marine Industries Limited of Sorel for approximately $12 million. The work will be performed, I believe, at the rate of a quarter each year over a period of four years. I am informed that it is over a period of five years.
What is the total amount for that contract dredging?

The total amount is
$13,021,000. Perhaps I might give the committee the places where the work is going to be done, as recommended by the committee. At Bellmouth Curve, there is 1,100,000 cubic yards of dredging material to be removed; at Ste. Anne, 1,900,000 cubic yards; at the head

of lake St. Peter, 475,000 cubic yards; Nicolet-Port St. Francis, 1,750,000 cubic yards; Cap de la Madeleine, 400,000 cubic yards; Becan-cour shoals, 140,000 cubic yards; Bastiscan,

Then, the last vote under this section provides for work contemplated for 1952 by the St. Lawrence ship canal and the Montreal harbour committee in the nature of subsurface exploration and rock boring in the main river channel near the De Boucherville islands.

I thank the minister for that information. It is quite clear that there are large sums of money being spent now, and to be spent, in order to keep this ship channel 200 miles long dredged out, to widen it and make various improvements. Naturally, as those improvements are made the annual cost of dredging will increase, because there will be a much bigger area to keep in shape. I am not quarrelling with that at all, because there is no doubt that Montreal is one of our great ports. I presume it is as a result of this expenditure in pursuance of this plan that the Empress of Scotland was able to come up the river from Quebec within the last few days and dock at Montreal. I understand that she is the largest passenger vessel, probably the largest vessel of any kind, that has ever been able to make that trip.
Of course, this is a good thing for Montreal, but it is rather hard on the port of Quebec. I am surprised that Quebec has not made some protest about it.
They have. They came up here in a delegation.

However, I would point out that the port of Montreal-I am quoting now from the national harbours board report for the year 1951-had a total of 4,423 incoming vessels in the year 1951, of which 1,188 were deep-sea vessels and 3,159 were coastal or inland commercial vessels including fishing boats, and 76 are described as "others". The total tonnage handled in Montreal harbour last year amounted to 14,917,040 tons, and the total grain receipts amounted to 110,143,566 bushels. I bring those figures out because there is a similar problem arising on the west coast with regard to Canada's other great harbour. I refer, of course, to the harbour of Vancouver. Here in the east we have millions of dollars being spent to maintain a harbour at Montreal, and with that I am not quarrelling. The minister said that under this plan there are to be capital expenditures of 55704-159
Supply-Transport
between $13 million and $14 million, and in addition to that there is the huge annual expenditure for dredging.
The port of Vancouver has more ships incoming and outgoing than the port of Montreal. The figures for last year show a total of 30,789 incoming, as compared with Montreal's 4,423. We had 1,231 ocean-going ships, as compared with Montreal's 1,188. In cargo tonnage we were somewhat smaller, our figure being 11,157,900 tons as compared with the 14,917,040 tons for Montreal. With regard to grain, the figures for Vancouver are 88,156,729 bushels as against more than 110 million bushels for Montreal. These two ports handle by far the largest proportion of the grain. They are far ahead of all the other ports in Canada put together in business handled.
Unfortunately, we have only a 35 foot channel through the narrows into Vancouver harbour and in order to accommodate the largest ships, and particularly the largest new tankers, we have to have the harbour entrance dredged a further 5 feet.
When I raised this matter the other night, the minister said he was not sure whether his department had made any representations to the Department of Public Works. Perhaps he has been able to check up on that in the meantime. I cannot urge too strongly that the Department of Transport make strong representations to the Department of Public Works that this dredging be undertaken at the earliest possible moment.
I would hope that a vote could be included in the supplementary estimates so we will not lose another year. We expect to have an oil pipe-line terminus built in the Vancouver area shortly, and there are plans for tank farms on the harbour shores. Unless these tankers can go in through the narrows, the port is going to be severely handicapped. As I said, I do not quarrel with Montreal. I am glad to see that they have their development. I feel sorry for the port of Quebec. 1 think it has had a pretty raw deal down through the years. It is a great tragedy-and it is brought home to me whenever I go to that most interesting city in Canada-that so much of the water traffic has passed it by and gone to Montreal.
On the west coast we have this extremely serious situation with which I am sure the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond will agree, as these tank farms are to be installed in his riding. I hope the minister will make representations to his colleague about this dredging and that we can expect something to be done along that line.

I was not able to say a great deal the other evening because the members of the harbours board were in Vancouver. They had been there for some weeks on a regular inspection trip. I will find out what the position is. They have probably discussed it with the port manager. Perhaps I can have something to say when we get on the national harbours board item later on.

May I point out to the minister that the distance to be dredged is not great. It would not be more than half or perhaps three-quarters of a mile. The cost is small change compared with the money that is being spent in keeping up and developing the port of Montreal.

I would bring to the attention of the minister the fact that the tank farm of the Trans Mountain oil line will be situated in my riding and that there is a situation with regard to the second narrows bridge. 482. Repairs and expenses in connection with the operation and maintenance of official railway cars under the jurisdiction of the department, $54,700.
Will the minister explain this item.

Yes. This is an annual item that is put in the estimates for the cost of operation, maintenance, running repairs and general overhaul of five official railway cars. These cars are assigned to the Department of Transport for administrative services. Cars Nos. 1 and 2 are for the use of the governor general. Car No. 100 is assigned to the Prime Minister. Car No. 101 is assigned to the cabinet ministers and distinguished visitors. Car No. 104 is assigned to the Minister of Transport. There are seven car stewards paid from this appropriation, and it may be broken down as follows: total salaries, $21,200; materials and supplies, $4,000; repairs and upkeep of equipment, $27,500; sundries, $2,000. There is an increase of $2,700 which is attributable almost exclusively to increases in salaries and cost of materials.
Surely this is one place where there could be some saving. As I remember it, we had only four of these cars a year or two ago.
Oh, no. The position with reference to these cars has not changed since I have been in the Department of Transport, and I am sure there was no change for a long time before that. There are five cars.
I have no quarrel with the cars for the governor general and for the Prime Minister; but why on earth should we have to have a car for the Minister of Transport?
Is there no gravy at all in this job?
Or why should we have one for the Minister of Public Works?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, I have no car.

The Minister of Public Works has a right to the use of one. The ministers get in this car and ride around the country any time they want to, and so do other members of the cabinet. We have travelling expenses. We have the cabinet going by air. When the Minister of Transport travels, I imagine he usually goes by air. When the Minister of National Defence travels, he seems to go by R.C.A.F. I suggest that the time has come to take another look at this vote. We are apparently keeping these five cars and keeping the staffs. In addition to that, somebody has to pay for hauling these cars on the railways.
They are hauled by the railways at their expense.
Do the railways have to haul them free?
They do not have to do it, but they do it.
There is no provision, legally, under which the railways must haul these cars free, but they do it as a courtesy?
That is right.
I do not want to hurt the feelings of the Minister of Transport, but I suggest that ordinary cabinet ministers could just as well travel by drawing room.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On foot.
Perhaps the Minister of Public Works could go by foot. If he does not have a few more bridges built, he will have to swim.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I could do that too.
I suggest that this is an unnecessary expense and that this item, instead of being increased, should be cut down.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I suggest that the position taken by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra should be given further consideration. I wonder whether we are not just carrying on a tradition that has been established, and doing so for no other reason than that it is established. There was a time when it was thought that certain important people should have special opportunities and privileges such as these. But with the way travel in ordinary sleeping cars has been improved, together with the improvements in air travel and in automobile travel, I wonder whether it is necessary to continue to maintain, at public expense, five official cars for use in this private way. The Minister of Public Works denied that he ever got a chance at these cars. I am not at all surprisedi-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: When I need one, I ask for it and I get it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Well, which is it? Does he, or does he not, use these cars? I imagine that most of the travel that is done by most of the ministers is not in private cars but just in ordinary sleeping car accommodation, or by air or by automobile. The conditions of travel have changed tremendously since the early days when this tradition was established. I do not know when this practice was first inaugurated; I suppose it was as early as we had railways in this country. Possibly it would be indiscreet to go the whole way and say "Cut them all out," 55704-1594
Supply-Transport
although I feel that way. But perhaps we should keep the one for the governor general.
Two.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Two, is it? I am not sure that even these need to be kept. At any rate, let us take another look at this practice. If we keep one or two, or even three, surely that is enough. I suggest the item is one in connection with which some saving could be effected, and I think it would be more in keeping with the spirit of the times, rather than keeping up this ancient tradition.

I just thought I might say a word on this. After all, this is not a very large item in the estimates. Of the cars involved two of them are for the governor general. Personally I think most Canadians would agree that that is certainly a proper provision. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said he had no quarrel with the Prime Minister having a car. I certainly agree with that. Therefore the question really reduces itself to whether or not we should spend any money to keep the other two cars which are available for the other members of the cabinet.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, that on balance I think it is probably an economic thing to have these cars available for the members of the cabinet. The possibility of using a private car for a trip on departmental business gives the minister an opportunity to do a certain amount of work and necessary business.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What about parliamentary assistants?
The parliamentary assistants do not get private cars. I am not speaking for myself.	,
Not yet.
No, and I do not think there is any possibility that they ever will.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Why discriminate?
The responsibilities of a minister and the demands on his time are very much greater than those on any parliamentary assistant, and I think we can get along very well.
Don't forget that.

Because of the responsibilities the ministers have, and the demands on their time, it is an economic thing and in the national interest to make it possible for them to travel with the facilities and iff the comfort provided by a private car.
We hear a great deal of carping criticism in this house about travelling expenses of ministers. I can speak for the people of

Supply-Transport
Halifax, I think with confidence. They like to see the ministers travel around this country and get firsthand knowledge of what is going on in Halifax, and Vancouver. If the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra does not want them to go out to Vancouver, I am sure his constituents would like to see the ministers of the crown taking an interest in what is going on in the parts of this country that are far removed from Ottawa. The money they spend on travelling expenses is very well invested in the national interest.

Just before the minister replies I would like to say a word. I must agree with the two hon. members on this side of the house who have spoken. I do not underestimate for a moment the value of privacy for members of the cabinet when they are travelling across the country to do necessary work, but I think the argument put up by the hon. member for Halifax who just took his seat is not very sound. I can recall that since I have been here a great number of cabinet ministers have gone to different parts of Canada, and they did not use private cars. I do not mean to suggest that when they do very important travelling without the use of a private car they neglect their work. I am quite sure they would not do that.
Certainly people in different parts of Canada like to see their ministers travel around and visit them and see what is going on. I would like to see the Minister of Transport visit Calgary and spend an evening at the C.N.R. station. If he did that I would not have to argue so much for a new station. But I do not think he needs a special car; in fact I doubt very much whether he would want one on such an occasion. It does seem to me that it does not add to the prestige of a minister because he happens to travel in a private car. In fact I think it would improve his popularity if he were to take a compartment in a train. He should have that; he should have some privacy where he can conduct his business. Certainly it would not cost the country as much for a compartment or a drawing room in a train as it would to carry a special coach. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has made a suggestion, and I think the department would do well to reconsider this item and see if some expenditure could not be saved in this country.	[DOT]

Has the
minister any information on hand as to the number of times each of these cars was used during the past year and the number of miles it travelled? I have a great deal of sympathy with the minister because on occasion I suppose he must travel with

the general manager and the chief engineer in order to inspect the railway. I do not know whether he does that, but I know that in Newfoundland we had one car which was used for that sort of thing, and it was very useful. No, I cannot answer that question, but I can answer it in another way. I can answer it in such a way that I think it will make those who have opposed this vote look rather foolish. I hesitate to do this, but I warn my hon. friends that I am going to do it, and they will take the responsibility for it.
I have been in the department for almost eight years. This is the first time in my experience that this vote has been opposed.
Oh, no.
Oh, yes.

While I am not going to argue in favour of the position in so far as I am concerned, I am going to say this. Out of this vote of $54,700, $20,000 only is provided for the car used by the Prime Minister, car 101 used by others in the cabinet and car 104 for the Minister of Transport, so we are arguing about $20,000; that is all we are arguing about. That vote has been far more than it is today. It has been as high as $83,000 in the past, and it has been reduced considerably. A private car was provided in former days for the deputy minister of transport. That has been eliminated. Are we going to quibble about $20,000 in so far as these cars are concerned, particularly when very often it is necessary, in fact it is important, for the Prime Minister and other ministers to have a private car at their disposal so they can, as the hon. member for St. John's West said, bring railway officials with them.
I am embarrassed by having to defend this vote, but I do want the committee to know that it is not $54,700 we are arguing about; it is $20,000. That is what we are arguing about. If my hon. friends want to argue about that, let them go to it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
What bothers me about the minister's remarks just now is that it does not matter what suggestion we make for saving a few dollars we are met with resistance. We are often told-somebody over there is saying it now-that it is small, that it is only $20,000. Well, to most people

in Canada $20,000 is still a fair chunk of money. We are told frequently that the savings we would suggest are only one or two per cent-and I hear the hon. member for Regina City talking about peanuts.
Peanuts for the C.C.F.

In my opinion, instead of saying something that was going to be hard for us on the opposition side to take, I think the Minister of Transport strengthened our case. I do not know what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra had in mind, or whether I am stealing his thunder-and I am quite prepared to let him have it-but I have written out an amendment which would reduce this item by $20,000.

I move, as I indicated-
That item 482 be reduced by $20,000.

My understanding of the statement by the Minister of Transport is that if this vote were reduced by $20,000 there would still be provision for two cars for the governor general and a car for the Prime Minister.
No; if this amendment were to pass the car of the Prime Minister and the other two cars would disappear. There would be provision only for the cars of the governor general.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

the provision for the cars for the governor general or for the Prime Minister. You are very petty in bringing it up", because that was the inference to be drawn from the remarks of the hon. member from Halifax. Someone else will say that this is just carping criticism. Well, the answer to that is that this is all money that has to be found.

We believe that this vote could be reduced. We believe it could be, reasonably.

We believe that this vote could be reduced.

speechtext: And that is the subamendment of the official opposition.

Have we lost our sense of proportion around here? We are running a four and a half billion dollar business in Canada, and that is a lot of money. It takes a lot of time and effort to spend that much money intelligently. When I think of nineteen top executives, apart from the Prime Minister, in connection with whose travelling we are trying to save $10,000, I am forced to the conclusion that it is just simply ridiculous.
I know of many company executives in British Columbia who do not do a hundredth part of the business these men do, but who are permitted to spend far more money for private automobiles and private travel than we allow our cabinet members.
When I look over at the government benches I often feel grateful. Let me add, in passing, that I am not in the habit of polishing apples; but when I look over there and see what these gentlemen do for the small salaries they receive; when I think of the miseries they endure, all for $18,000 a year, I think the whole thing is ridiculous. And if, by any chance, those gentlemen keep their jobs and work for such small salaries, even if some money is spent for private cars for their use, I think it is the cheapest form of salary we could pay them. In short, I think we are paying them in brass instead of gold.

I believe one point is being missed in this discussion, and that the stand taken by hon. members on this side of the house has been misinterpreted. It should be remembered that perhaps fifty years ago private cars were about the only means of long-range travel which could be put at the disposal of members of the cabinet. At the present time, however, there are other

means of travel which have come into widespread use. I am reasonably certain that the cost of transportation of cabinet ministers has increased considerably in the last fifty years. Even the suggested reduction would not bring the amount to anything near as low a figure as it was fifty years ago.
Other means of transportation are frequently used, and perhaps used more efficiently. I have in mind air transportation, and transportation by automobile. To have a balanced view of the whole matter one should take all these means of transportation into consideration. My feeling is that the use of private railway cars has become almost obsolete as a means of travel. Considering what is paid to maintain it, this means of travel is not used very much. The benefit derived by cabinet ministers is out of all proportion to the cost.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: BURRARD INLET TUNNEL AND BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 239, respecting the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should say, to start with, that I am sponsoring this bill as the member for Coast-Capilano and not as the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance. The Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company is a publicly owned company whose shares are held jointly by the city of North Vancouver, the district of North Vancouver, the district of West Vancouver and the city of Vancouver. The company owns the bridge which is commonly called the second narrows bridge, which spans the upper end of Vancouver harbour connecting Vancouver and North Vancouver. The bridge was built in 1925 and was the first connection with the north shore by bridge. The central span was knocked down in 1930 by a steamer, and the Vancouver harbours board then advanced $900,000 to reconstruct the bridge and change the bascule span into a lift span. The Vancouver harbour commission took over the operation of the bridge until this debt should be repaid, and that was only last year; so the bridge has only recently returned to the possession of the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company.
The main reason for this bill is that the company is at the present time negotiating with the Canadian National Railways for a twenty-one year lease of the rail lines across that bridge to the C.N.R. The company intend to keep in their own possession the roadway on which tolls are charged. Section 2 of this bill is in its present form to show quite clearly that charges on the rail right of way and on the road right of way can be separated. The only other point is that the representatives on the board of directors until now have included the mayors or reeves of each of those towns. They would rather have the decision left to the council concerned whether it should be the mayor or some alderman.
Then in the third clause they have changed the name "Vancouver Harbour Commissioners" to "National Harbours Board," which has taken over the Vancouver harbour commission's operation' of many years ago, and they give the proper description to two other railway companies.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. May I ask hon. members to refrain from speaking or interjecting, because if I am to follow the remarks 

which are being made by the hon. member I must at least hear what he has to say. From what I hear I am almost of the same opinion as I was when the hon. member was speaking to this clause in a general way on the last occasion. I have listened to him again this evening. He introduced the subject by saying he was going to speak about the confusion of a political party having regard to the national policy on gas. I am quite willing to give him as much latitude as other hon. members have taken on this clause, but I do not think that we should hear a review of the policies advocated by the various political parties in this house.

My remarks have a very important bearing on this bill we are now considering. I explained on May 2 that under a national gas policy the Progressive Conservative members of parliament are opposed to the incorporation of the Boundary Pipeline Corporation.
One of the basic tenets of a national policy on gas is that natural gas, like all the other host of natural resources in Canada's ten provinces, should be utilized to bring the maximum possible benefits to the provinces containing the resources, and maximum benefits to Canada as a whole. We recognize, of course, that provinces containing natural resources have every right and every duty to fully protect their own long-term supplies before making their surplus available to other provinces or other outsiders. The Progressive Conservative party in Alberta is already on record as supporting gas export.
Never heard of it.

The rate of gas discovery is such that we believe the time has come to make the fast growing surplus available to others. The reasons for supporting gas export are partly selfish, for we know that exports will bring to Alberta a measure of industrial growth and prosperity dwarfing that which could or might come from any "keep the gas for Alberta" policy. The Alberta Liberal party, on the other hand, has through its leader, Harper Prowse, and other spokesmen, been damning gas exports and calling them the great betrayal of the people of Alberta.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

decided that pipe line companies would have to come before this parliament to be incorporated. At that time the hon. member might have been in order if he had discussed the views of the various political parties throughout the country on this important matter.
But as it stands today, even if a general discussion is allowed I cannot see how the policies advocated by the provincial parties or national parties in the House of Commons can have anything to do with the bill before us. The national policy in this connection is not under discussion.

Your Honour did not question the statement on this subject by the hon. member for Vegreville when this bill was last up for discussion. At that time he dealt with nothing but the political policy in Alberta.
Mr. Chairman-

Boundary Pipeline Corporation

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have not before me the citation which applies in this instance. However, so far as my memory goes I do not think any expression used by the hon. member so far has been termed unparliamentary. However, if as between one member and another the hon. member for Calgary West wishes to please the hon. member for Charlotte, he could use another expression. I do not think, however, that according to the rules it is unparliamentary. I do not recall that the expression has been so ruled.

The term I used was
"roughshod". I might say that steps were taken to prevent the hearing of crossexamination and evidence that I believe would have clearly established that the Boundary project is not economic. The Liberal member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine suddenly moved, during the cross-examination of Boundary's engineer, that the committee-
-has obtained sufficient evidence to decide on the economic practicability of the pipe line under consideration and that the question be now put on the preamble without further examination of witnesses.
His motion was seconded by the Liberal member for Notre Dame de Grace, and the motion was put through by the Liberals, despite the opposition of every member of other parties on that committee, and the opposition of one good Liberal member, the hon. member for Hastings South. The Liberal majority thereby forced' approval by the committee of incorporation of a pipe line company which on several grounds fails to meet the best interests of Alberta or Canada.
In opposing incorporation of Boundary, the Progressive Conservatives are not attempting to delay eastward gas export from Alberta, or delay gas supply to the provinces east of Alberta. Two companies, with eastward pipe line plans much larger than those of Boundary and much sounder economically, have already been incorporated; and we believe the choice should be between the two alternative routes they offer, in order to get gas to eastern Canada in addition to the eastern prairies.
The backers of both these incorporated companies, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines and Western Pipe Lines Company, have already spent many millions of dollars in western gas exploration and development, and are still busily engaged in discovering gas reserves to supply part of their expected requirements. The backers of Boundary have provided no evidence that they are contributing anything to the discovery of gas for the pipe line they propose. There are good reasons for doubting that a pipe line from southern Alberta to serve the cities and towns of southern Saskatchewan and Manitoba would be economical. In other words it is doubtful whether it could
[ Mr, Nickle.l
serve a large enough market or deliver gas at a low enough price to compete with other fuels and obtain adequate revenue to recover its cost.
To be more specific, Boundary presented a brief setting out costs of its Alberta to Winnipeg line at just over $28 million. Without presenting any proof whatsoever of its figures for the gas market, and without in fact even making a detailed economic survey of the potential markets, Boundary assumed it could sell gas for an average wholesale price of under 28 cents per thousand cubic feet. Using Boundary's own construction cost figures and basing the gas market upon the detailed economic studies made by Western Pipe Lines, I advised the railway committee that in order to earn 6 j per cent on its investment Boundary would have to charge an average wholesale price of 811 cents per thousand cubic feet during its first year, and by the fifth year would still have to charge over 37 cents. When it is considered that Boundary's principal market would be industries in Winnipeg which now get lignite coal at a delivered cost equivalent to only 30 cents per thousand cubic feet of gas there seems to be little hope that gas delivered by Boundary's line going no further than Winnipeg could capture the market from coal.
On the other hand, if Saskatchewan and Manitoba cities were provided with gas from a major pipe line extending to large markets in eastern Canada or the United States the delivered cost of gas to prairie communities would be considerably lower. Such major pipe lines would give Saskatchewan and Manitoba domestic and commercial markets gas at reasonable cost, though it is doubtful that even a major pipe line could capture from cheap lignite coal and hydro power the larger industrial market of Winnipeg.
I indicated earlier that Boundary has not made what could be called an adequate economic survey of its proposed route to Winnipeg. Fortunately several detailed economic surveys of potential gas markets in Saskatchewan and Manitoba have been made over the past two years by sponsors of other pipe line projects and by the distributor of artificial gas in Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think the amount of gas allocated by the Alberta government for export to the Pacific coast justifies the building of a pipe line?

The answer to that is no, because the percentage allocated from the Peace river district coupled with roughly a trillion cubic feet of gas now believed proved in the Peace river area of British Columbia

Boundary Pipeline Corporation plus, I hope within a very few months or maybe sooner, approval of more gas from the Peace river area of Alberta, will justify that Pacific coast line. Second, the Boundary project, even if it were economic, would penalize consumers of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. A small scale line would have to sell gas at substantially higher prices than would a major project such as those proposed by Trans-Canada and Western. Third, acceptance of the Boundary project could delay, perhaps for years, the securing of gas in large volume by Ontario and Quebec either by direct pipe line from Alberta or by gas exchange with the United States.
As a member of this parliament I shall not be a party to approving incorporation of a pipe line company that has failed to establish a sound economic basis for its project. As an Albertan I shall not support a project which could both delay and reduce the industrial development of my province. As a Canadian I shall oppose Boundary's incorporation because I prefer that Saskatchewan and Manitoba shall get lower priced gas than Boundary could offer, and believe that Ontario and Quebec should not be barred from the advantages of a reasonable cost, highly convenient fuel such as natural gas.
