There is one other thing I want to say before I sit down. As far back as I can remember-and I can remember the period before the election of 1911-this flag waving has taken place. In fact it has been going on since confederation. When members stand up in the house and suggest no truck nor trade with the Yankees I and most other maritimers resent such a statement. Since the turn of the century and up until the last few years the people of Alberta depended exclusively on the United States of America for the gas and oil they consumed. Right across Canada we were faced with the same situation. Did you ever hear anyone in the United States say: No gas or oil for the Dominion of Canada; keep it under the ground down here.
During the last war, which is not too long ago, the allocation of oil to Canada by the United States was more liberal in many cases than what was provided for their own citizens. I said in the committee and I repeat now that I remember reading in the press on many occasions during the last war that the people of Boston were sitting in their

homes in fur coats because of a lack of fuel oil for their furnaces. To my knowledge that situation did not arise in the maritime provinces from where I come. We were provided with oil, gas and fuel oil by our good friends to the south.
Just a few nights ago I listened to a radio address by the mayor of Calgary. I should have liked a copy of his address so I could put it on the record. He stated definitely that the only way gas could ever be provided for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec was to bring in the gas from Texas and export the surplus gas of western Canada across the border to the United States. Any fair-minded man who looks at the situation knows that is the only thing that can be done. Reciprocity is the only consideration at the present time. The idea of oil and gas only for Canadians and no truck nor trade with the Yankees just does not go with maritimers. I have the same opinion now that I had when I sat as a member of the committee. I believe the witnesses who appeared there presented a good story. I believe the evidence they produced was authentic, and I believe it carries more weight than the evidence produced by the hon. member for Calgary West. I do not believe there was any steamrolling at any time, or that anyone was run over roughshod. We had a Liberal majority in the committee and we carried on in exactly the way the people of this country want us to carry on.

In the second place, unless a lot of people change their way of doing things there just will not be any gas or oil to export.
We in the province of Alberta have been keenly interested in the development of our great resources in such a way as to contribute to the strength of Canada and the well-being of the Canadian people because we felt it was in the interests of Canada and its people to do so. We have wanted to develop the gas and oil resources so that all parts of Canada can benefit from them. We do not look upon these resources as belonging entirely to the people of the province of Alberta, not by any means. Nor do we for one moment, Mr. Chairman, make the claim that it was solely through the genius of the Social Credit government of Alberta that the development occurred, although some people have attempted to make that claim. I doubt very much if the political situation will ever make it possible for the gas to be exported from the province. Altogether too much of an irresponsible nature has been said in this house and elsewhere about the export of gas from Alberta. It is seriously interfering with logical thought by people everywhere and, as I said, may result in no gas being made available. This would be a serious situation, if gas surplus to the needs of Alberta is found in reserve. I say it in all seriousness, and I should like to see a whole lot less foolish and irresponsible talk and a lot more careful thought given to this problem.

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT Railway and steamship service-
492. Degaussing and strengthening of sea-going merchant ships of Canadian registry of 1,000 gross tons and over, $500,000.

May I reply to two or three questions that were asked earlier, and get them out of the way. The hon. member for St. John's West inquired as to the names of the steamship inspectors. There are three, Mr. De Valliant, Mr. Barrett, and one whose appointment is still pending. Then I believe the hon. member for Cape Breton South wanted a breakdown of the expenses including those for Canadian distressed seamen. The total is $6,240.58 of which $2,080.56 was paid by ship owners under distressed seamen's regulations and the balance by the department.
Then the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre wanted me to take one of the items of the department and indicate to what extent we had spent the money estimated in the previous year. I took the item of canals, the one concerning operation and maintenance during the last five years. In the fiscal year 1947-48 the estimates were $3,224,000. I may say that I am giving round figures only. We spent $3,215,000. In 1948-49 the estimate was $3,705,000; we spent the full amount. In 1949-50 the estimate was $2,908,000; we spent the full amount. In 1950-51 it was $4,328,000. We spent $4,248,000. In 1951-52 it was $4,678,000 and we spent $4,596,000.

At six o'clock I asked that item 492 be left over until now because I think this half million dollars in this estimate means some addition to government policy. Some of us know about degaussing from the last war. In looking at last year's estimates I do not find in them a dollar to cover the matter of degaussing. Before I ask a couple more
Supply-Transport
questions, will the minister explain just what the government's policy is on this matter?

Since the end of the war there has never been in the estimates any item for degaussing; but in September of last year we decided that ships of 1,000 gross registered tons or over, being built for Canadian registry, should be fitted at government expense with degaussing equipment as a protection against magnetic mines and with under-deck stiffening above which defensive guns could be mounted in an emergency. As a result of this decision we are fitting with this equipment five ships, three of them now building in Canadian yards and two in United Kingdom yards for Canadian registry; and we are at the same time undertaking a survey of all other ships to ascertain what the cost will be. By "all other ships" I mean the 44 war-built, 10,000-ton Park vessels and the twelve 4,700-ton freighters. These vessels were all fitted with this equipment during the last war. The point is to what extent the equipment is serviceable at this time. That survey has not been completed. The object of this estimate is to have the funds available in case of necessity.

I think the minister is to be complimented on his foresight in this matter. As I say, some of us on the west coast, from our experience during the last war, know just what degaussing did for our merchant navy. As I say, I think the minister is to be complimented on his forward outlook in this whole matter.
Would the minister mind putting on the record a definition of the word "degaussing".

My understanding of it is that ships are to be fitted with equipment for the detection of mines. During the last war this equipment consisted of an electric cable which sets off a current and thereby does not attract the mine.

As I understand the minister this evening, this vote covers only work to be done on five new ships, three of which are building in Canadian yards and two in United Kingdom yards. That is contrary to the press reports at the time the estimates were brought down. They indicated that all the old ocean-going ships were to be fitted with degaussing equipment and were also to be strengthened, and that some of the coastal ships were to be improved in the same manner. May we have that point cleared up?
I have not seen the press reports to which my hon. friend refers.

It was when the Minister of Finance brought down his estimates.

Supply-Transport

This vote covers not only five ships but all existing ships that will be built after the date of the approval of the policy, which was in September of 1951; that is, ships of over 1,000 tons gross register. I refer to those five because they are new ones. There will be other new ships that it will also cover. The intention is also to cover existing ships. A survey is being made to ascertain what will be the cost. That survey is in progress now.
What about coastal ships? Are they to be handled in the same way?
If they come within this definition, they would be. If they are new ships, yes.
I do not understand where the minister draws the line between doing this work on new ships and on old ships. Is he planning to do it on the present old cargo vessels?

What I am saying is that the decision covers ships to be built in the future, and a survey is being made to ascertain what the cost will be on the other ships I have mentioned. When that cost is known and that survey is completed, a decision will be taken as to those ships.
Then I understand that at the moment the policy is only to do the ships which are built after a date in September?
That is right.
How are these expenses met? Do the owners of these ships have to pay anything or does the government bear the whole cost?
In so far as new ships are concerned, we are paying the whole cost. In so far as other ships are concerned, we shall have to determine that question when we get the report.
Why does the government assume that cost? Under what law can the ship companies be compelled to have this work done to their ships even though the government pays the cost?
We did it during the last war, and we did it on the basis of national defence. It is on that basis that we are proceeding now.
Will the ship companies be under any obligation to turn their ships over to the government in time of war? Is there some string attached to it in the event of a war breaking out?
No, there is not.
Is the navy to have anything to do with this plan, or is it being handled entirely by the Department of Transport?
It is being handled by the Department of National Defence, and we cover it by an estimate in our department.
Then the Department of National Defence is having this war work done on these ships but the vote comes through the Department of Transport?
Yes.
Why is that not a defence vote?
I presume because the ships are part of the merchant navy.

How many ships will this
amount of money cover?

That is what I am not able to say. I can tell from time to time how many ships it will cover, because we have a record of them, but I cannot tell how many old ships it will cover until the survey is over.
Is there a set figure of cost for each ship? The vote is for $500,000. How many ships is it expected will be covered by that vote?
It should cover about ten new ships, and some of the ships that the survey will report upon.

Do these 10 ships include
passenger ships, or are they all cargo vessels?
Well, it would include all the ships, I should think, that the survey would report upon, and I presume that will include all ships of the Park vessel type, and the 4,700 tonners.
New passenger ships as well as freighters?
Yes.

The item reads:
Degaussing and strengthening of sea-going merchant ships . . .
Does that mean setting up the gun emplacements?
Gun stiffening, yes.
That is what is meant?
That is correct.

Is any of the
degaussing equipment that was installed in merchant ships during the war still in serviceable condition, or has it been dismantled?
Yes, there is quite a considerable amount on ships. Some of it is in pretty fair condition; on others not, and that is the object of making the survey.

I have been waiting for this one. I should like to bring a specific problem to the minister's attention, having to do with a small group of employees who come within the scope of his department. I refer to the section of the corps of commissionaires who are employed at airports under the Department of Transport.
The corps of commissionaires consists of quite a large group of ex-servicemen over forty years of age. They are employed by different departments of government. The income tax department employs some of them. All these categories working for certain departments of government enjoy certain rights and privileges. At the airports that come under the Department of Transport all the employees who are working for transport, if they commute to work, have the right to receive $11.40 a month as a rebate in lieu of transportation, with the exception of the corps of commissionaires. There are not many of them. There may be half a dozen around each airport.
I have taken this matter up with the department. It is not new. I have taken it up on a couple of occasions. The last occasion was on March 6 of this year. The minister wrote to me and said that while he was sympathetic, this particular group of corps of commissionaires employed by the Department of Transport on airports were working under the R.C.M.P., and he was referring my communication to the Department of Justice. Well, that was on March 6. I have heard nothing from the Department of Justice on the matter. I am bringing this to the minister's attention because I do not think that group of commissionaires, who are working for transport on these airports, should be the responsibility of the Department of Justice. They work directly for the Department of Transport and should be under the supervision of the officials of that department and those in charge of the local stations.

Dealing first with the latter point, we have a number of districts where there are interference cars. There is a vote dealing with that a little later, but perhaps I can answer my hon. friend now if I am permitted to do so. We do a considerable amount of work all across the country. We send out these inspectors when advice is received that there is interference. The inspectors go first to the complainant. Then they go about the area with their car to try to identify the equipment that is causing the interference, and about 80 per cent of the time they succeed in doing so. They report to the complainant, and then they indicate as courteously as they can to the person who is responsible for the interference that it should be removed and how it can be removed.
My hon. friend raised the question of additional inspectors, particularly in the district of Kelowna, British Columbia. It is a fact that the inspector at Kelowna has a large territory to cover. However, it is a costly matter, and it would be uneconomical to provide inspectors throughout Canada in sufficient numbers to visit every community frequently. The department of course depends to a large extent upon the co-operation of electrical equipment dealers and public utility companies who make reports from time to time to our inspectors in the area. However, I shall be glad to take my hon. friend's remarks under consideration and see if we cannot assist that particular area.

May I suggest that the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Public Works might get together and send an inspector around some of the corridors of the parliament buildings to try to detect some of the inferior electric razors that are being used throughout the building.	[DOT]

What powers do these inspectors have to enforce action to eliminate interference? After they have gone out and located the interference, what powers have they to see that the person who is responsible takes action to correct it? I have in mind a case in Alberta where a complaint was laid. The inspector arrived and finally located where the interference came from but apparently that was as far as he went. He notified the person that his little power plant was responsible for the interference, but no action was taken.

The answer is that I do not think the inspectors have any powers. They do it as a service. They act because they are so requested, and I do not think they could tell an offending person that he must eliminate the interference. All they can do is to communicate to the complainant

what is the cause and point out to the offending party the way to eliminate it. I think if they were to go any further they would be interfering with property and civil rights.

There might be, but I do not know under what legislation it could be enforced. I think these things have to be done by education and by asking people to co-operate with us. We find that out of the large number of cases investigated 80 per cent, if not more, do co-operate.

The case of interference which I should like to mention is a little different from the type of interference discussed by the last few speakers. It relates to the way in which one station in Winnipeg seems to prevent people from hearing another station. May I say to the minister that I have taken the matter up with Mr. Dunton, the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and he indicated to me that the matter is really one that comes under the Department of Transport. Nevertheless he was familiar with the problem and wrote me in reply to my representations. I appreciated Mr. Dun-ton's letter, and I appreciate the fact that the m-atter of allotting channels so that everyone will get a hearing seems to be a problem that is difficult to solve. The Winnipeg station to which I refer particularly is CKY, which is at 580 kilocycles. To give the whole picture perhaps I should indicate that the Winnipeg stations are CKY at 580; CKRC at 630; CBW at 990; CKSB at 1250 and CJOB at 1340. So far as I can ascertain none of these Winnipeg stations interfere with each other. They -are well placed, and that is fairly good considering that this adds up to five stations in the Winnipeg area. However, there are Winnipeg people who like to be able to tune in on one or other of the major United States networks. The nearest outlet for the NBC network is KFYR in Bismarck, North Dakota, at 550. The nearest outlet for the Columbia network is KSJB at 600, which is in Jamestown, North Dakota. It is in connection with KSJB at 600 and CKY Winnipeg a-t 580 that we get into difficulty. In the other cases there seems to be no difficulty, but the people who want to listen to the Columbia network through KSJB at 600 tell me they are frequently prevented from doing so because of interference from CKY at 580.
As I say, I have taken the matter up with Mr. Dunton but as yet no solution to the

problem seems to have been found. It is a case of interference which is different from the other types of interference members have been talking about. Mr. Dunton does say the matter comes under the Department of Transport. Can the minister say whether his officials have looked into this matter and considered whether any other arrangement can be made or anything done to rectify this situation?

Indeed they have, Mr. Chairman, but it is a very difficult problem and one which is not easy to solve. It is a difficult problem because it arises in every country, not only in Canada and the United States. The best method of reaching a solution is through the international conferences which take place from year to year. There is the North American regional broadcasting conference which sat at Montreal for some time and dealt in part with this question. It sat at Washington last year, and we have delegates to that conference whose duty and responsibility it is to try to iron out these difficulties. These conferences give consideration to the general question of interference between stations in the same country or between stations in one country and stations in another country. I believe that with the new technical developments it may be possible to stop the interference, but I do not know. I can assure the hon. member that our officers are seized with the problem and are doing the best they can to solve it.

Will the minister explain to the committee just what the department's policy now is with respect to the maintenance of telephone and telegraph service in various parts of the country?

The policy is to assist those people who reside in isolated parts of Canada. I do not want to select any one part more than another. We try to maintain telephone and telegraph services in remote sections, so as not to deprive any part of Canada of service, until such time as a private corporation can step in and take over. In certain areas of Quebec and the maritime provinces it has become a regular policy to assist municipalities and sometimes private corporations. On the west coast in British Columbia we are trying to divest ourselves of these operations because there is one company-if there are not two-showing interest in taking it over. If we can get a reasonable price for our facilities we will sell them. The main policy is to assist these isolated areas until such time as they can operate their own services.

I have reference now particularly to the lines in the Peace river country. I wanted first to tell the minister how much

those lines have meant to the people up in that great north country. For the past seven or eight years I have been fairly well acquainted with the work the transport people are doing up there.
I wonder if the minister has been made acquainted with the situation up at Keg River. I imagine it would take a little while to get the information on it, but here is the situation. The line runs across country from Peace River. It was intended, of course, to penetrate the great northwest and give service and communication on up into the Great Slave lake area. This little settlement-I do not know whether you would call it a settlement or not; it is not a village, just a settlement-at Keg River is one of the principal terminals on the route. It happens to be about ten miles off the main highway leading from Grimshaw north into the Slave lake area. As a consequence the line is not nearly as valuable in maintaining communication with the outside world as it might be if they had followed the main highway north a little bit more closely.
I know how costly it might be to change the location of the line. But here is your Mr. Herrington, who is the operator-and he has been in there for a good many years- living at the Keg River settlement, carrying on his work, sending in his weather observations every few hours, keeping in touch with the Peace River headquarters and all that sort of thing, and transmitting the information that needs to be transmitted back and forth. But the people who are travelling through that newly-opened country are passing along the highway ten miles to the east. At various times of the year it is difficult to get to that line or to any terminal in case of necessity. It is the only line up there. I was wondering whether some consideration might be given to moving the terminal up to the highway east of Cape river, so that better use could be made of it.
I want to compliment the people up there who are doing that work. They have done a fine job. That has been a service the people have greatly appreciated. I just wondered whether any consideration had been given to moving the line up along the highway.
I am not aware of the particular case to which my hon. friend refers, but I will take it under advisement now and will ask our officers to see if it cannot be done.
Thank you very much.

I want to thank the minister for the trouble he is taking. He can understand how anxious I am to do something for this widow whose husband lost his life in that plane accident. Surely there should be some compensation., or something done for the woman. I thank you, and I hope you will continue to try to get some information.
I will try to get something for you.
She is not able to afford legal assistance.

This afternoon I brought up the question of the possibility of having a crash boat or some life-saving service established at Sandspit on Queen Charlotte islands, and the minister was going to check on that point and let me know when this item came up for discussion.
I am sorry; I have not had an opportunity of doing it. As this discussion goes on perhaps I could speak to one of the officers here.

Another point has to do with the situation in Canada in so far as transport planes are concerned. I think that was raised during the discussion of the estimates last year. About a year and a half ago there was a good deal of concern because Canada had no reserve of transport planes available in the event of trouble. There was a discussion at that time of plans by which the government might acquire transport planes and turn them over to civilian operators on a loan or lease basis. Other plans were also considered. Can the minister tell us whether any such scheme is in operation or contemplation?

Yes. The government has that matter very seriously under consideration and it has done a number of things to assist the operators of commercial transport planes. I am not free to discuss them fully, because I hope before this session is over it will be possible to bring in an amendment to one of the acts, which will be of assistance.
Supp ly-Transport
Then I believe we did take action in the budgetary resolutions to facilitate the importation of planes from the United States. There is also under study now the question of whether or not it will be possible to assist the purchasers of these planes by way of additional depreciation. We feel that the suggestions I have indicated would be better than if the Department of National Defence were to buy them and hold them, or in the event of emergency turn them over to private companies.
Are we still very short of transport planes in Canada?
There has been a steady but slow increase in the number of these planes coming in.
But it is a definite policy of the government to take steps to increase the number of transport planes?
Yes, it is.

One other question: I understand there has been an application by Canadian Pacific Air Lines for permission to fly from Vancouver to South America. Would the minister tell the committee whether that application has been granted?

There is no such application. There is some talk of Canadian Pacific Air Lines flying to South America via the west coast. That, I presume, when it is determined, would have to be decided after agreement with the countries of South America. No formal application has been made, and we have made no representations to the government of Mexico. There has been no formal approach, although there has been some correspondence between the Department of External Affairs and the state department, or its equivalent, in Mexico. The matter is very much to the fore.
The government would approve the inauguration of such service?
I do not think there is any doubt about it.

Item agreed to.
Operation and maintenance-
512.	Civil aviation services, $9,325,320.
Does the department officially make investigation with respect to accidents to commercial aircraft?

Yes, we do. There is provision in the Aeronautics Act for the appointment of an investigator when a crash takes place.

Supply-Transport
Will there be any announcement of results before the publication of the annual report of the department? Do they appear anywhere else?

They appear in public
statements made by the minister. When the report has been completed and sent in. to the air transport board, they communicate it to the minister, and a public announcement of the findings is made.

Item agreed to.
513.	Airway and airport traffic control, $1,425,396.

The minister made reference to item 513 when he opened discussion on his estimates. I believe he said some of this expenditure was being made on behalf of the Department of National Defence. Why is that necessary? Why is it handled in that way?

The Department of National Defence have asked us to take over a number of airports, and they do ask us to take over airports from time to time. That is why a portion of this covers those airports. This obtains generally where there is traffic which is partly military and partly civil. In these airports the Department of National Defence asks us as a rule to take over the civil air operation of the airport.

Then I asked the minister if he could give us the valuation placed on the Vancouver airport by his valuator. He said he did not have that information at hand at the moment, but I understood he would make it available at a later date.

I do not think I can make that report available. It was a confidential report to me. I was asked for that same information by the mayor and municipal authorities of Vancouver; and, so that they would feel that nothing was being hidden, I sent them a summary covering I believe all the information they required. They seemed to be satisfied, because they did not ask for the report itself. In that summary is contained the figure for which the hon. member is asking. I cannot recall what it was, and would not like to give it from memory.
Press dispatches indicated that it was $1,503,000.
I would think that is probably correct.
Is it approximately correct?
I believe so; but I am speaking from memory, and it is several months since I have seen it.

What is the minister's objection to having this long-standing dispute referred
[Mr. Chevrier.)
to arbitration, or decided by the exchequer court. It seems to me unfortunate that it should drag on for three or four years without reaching any agreement. One result is that the city has not the money available to help build a new bridge to replace the Marpole bridge. I believe the council plan to use the money they get from the department for that purpose. What is the objection to having it arbitrated?

I do not think there is anything to arbitrate. I presume the city think we should buy the land. We have indicated to them we do not think we should. We are willing to pay a reasonable price for the buildings. It was on that basis that the offer was made. It may be that a compromise can be found. As indicated the other night, I understand some of the officials from Vancouver are coming down to discuss the matter further, and I shall welcome any discussion. Beyond that I cannot say more.
Why is a different position taken by the department with respect to that airport from that concerning the airport at Dorval, which I believe was paid for entirely by the department?

I indicated the other night that the position is the same with respect to all airports in Canada, where municipalities have contributed something. The only exception is Dorval, because of the transfer that was made from St. Hubert, which was a military airport, to Dorval. The government in those years felt it should purchase the land, and it did. That is the only exception.
The government has paid everything in connection with Dorval?
I understand it has.
How much has it cost, approximately?
I would not have that information on this item, but I can get it.
What about Malton?
A substantial contribution has been made there by the city of Toronto and, I believe, by the harbour commission. In fact, a large part of the property is still owned by Malton.

I do not wish to take up more time on it, but the minister knows that the Vancouver airport is an international airport. It is far beyond the position of being only a municipal airport. I do suggest the department should not stick to the position that it will pay nothing whatever for the land. It should be possible to reach some agreement.
We are giving it our best attention.

I should like -to say a few words about the matter which has just been discussed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra in connection with the Vancouver international airport. I am partly in agreement with what he -says. I certainly am in agreement with his statement that the Vancouver international airport is a very important airport. The figures given by me by Mr. William Inglis, the manager of the Vancouver airport, show that for the first three months of this year passengers out of that airport totalled 92,211, an increase of 16 per cent over the same period in the previous year; airmail amounted to 702,281 pounds, an increase of 23 per cent; air cargo amounted to 823,966 pounds, an increase of 14 per cent, and aircraft movements, which are the real indication of the business carried on by an airport, were 40,929, an. increase of 45 per cent.
Great things are going on at that airport and I want to compliment the minister upon what he has done in the way of improvements. At the present time we -are building a runway which will be the longest in Canada at a cost of something like $2 million. The investment of the government of Canada in that airport at the present time far outweighs the investment of the city of Vancouver.
I think the minister is making an error in attempting to draw a parallel between the Vancouver international airport and the development which has taken place at Malton or Dorval. In 1929 the city council of Vancouver, with far more foresight than they dreamed at that time, purchased some 475 acres of land to' form the nucleus of what is now an airport consisting of some 1,400 acres. They own only 475 acres. In the case of Malton there was an -agreement between Toronto and the department under which Toronto supplied the land and the federal government provided the investment necessary for capital improvement. I think more or less the same arrangement applied in the case of Dorval and Montreal.
As I say, the history of the purchase of Vancouver -airport goes back to 1929. In 1945 the city decided they wanted to retain control of the airport and it was returned to them at that time by the government. The city has been operating it since. They now wish to dispose of their interests in the airport, and they are asking for only the money which they have put into it.
I am informed that they are -agreeable to accepting $1,100,000 as a discharge of their investment. The minister has indicated that the city authorities are coming down to see him -shortly, an-d I hope -at that time he will feel disposed to take over full control 55704-161
Supply-Transport
of this airport and pay the -city $1,100,000. I do not think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra realizes that there has been a dispute among the city authorities. He must realize that a bylaw would have to be passed in -connection with this, and the authorities wanted to -arrive at a figure which they could recommend to the citizens of Vancouver.
As he knows, the first suggestion they made was that they should be paid $2,500,000. That sum was quite in excess of the investment of the city in the airport; it was quite in excess of the compounded losses, interest charges and retirement of debt on the bonds. As I say, I am informed that they are now agreeable to accepting $1,100,000. I must compliment the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra upon the agility he has shown from time to time in confusing the airport with the bridges which give access to the airport and which he and I both know are solely the responsibility of the province of British Columbia.
I do not agree with that.

If my hon. friend will study the agreement I think he will agree that at least the initiative must be taken by the province of British Columbia because the existing bridges are their full responsibility.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Let us confine ourselves to airports.

I am just concluding. I do hope that when the city fathers come down here shortly the minister will give them every consideration. We in that area are extremely proud of this airport, which is beginning to be heard about not only in Canada but throughout North America. It is going to be one of the great airports in North America. Next year Canadian Pacific Air Lines will begin service to the Orient, flying Constellations to Hawaii and then jets to the Orient. We should pay some attention to what is going on in the United States, where a recent merger has occurred between Capital Airlines and Northwest Airlines. I understand United States lines are in position today to sell through tickets from Florida to Tokyo.
We are justly proud in Canada of the great strides aviation is making. A report made recently by on p of the ministers indicates the great primary work done by tne Minister of Trade and Commerce in expanding Canada's air facilities. Canada is now the second nation in the world in point of air travel outside the country. That is a very proud position to have and we must see that we maintain it on the west coast as well as on the east coast. We can do that by continuing the excellent degree of

Supply-Transport
improvement and the providing of new facilities which is being carried on at the present time at Vancouver international airport. It is my thought that this work could be carried on more effectively if the government had full control.

Item agreed to.
Airways and airports-Construction services-
515. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment-capital, $7,517,450.

Is the
revenue for the use of airports collected by the department?
Yes, and paid over to the consolidated revenue fund.
It does not reduce this in any way?
No.

As most members know, Halifax means practically everything east of Moncton but it is without an airport able to handle the heavy transport planes. This means that a person going to Montreal from Halifax must shuttle back and forth in the smaller planes. We were greatly pleased when we heard the announcement that Halifax was to have a new airport and I was wondering if the minister could tell us the present status of these plans.

All I can say is that our people have made a survey of the site and it must be determined whether the weather conditions are such that we can operate at that site. That determination has not been made, but it is progressing.

I should like to associate myself with what my colleague has said with regard to our satisfaction at the statement the minister has made. Can the minister state whether the arrangements for the purchase of the site have been made, or just what the status is?
All I can say-no doubt my hon. friend knows this-is that the city are willing to make a contribution toward the purchase of the site. I cannot state exactly what that is.
There has been nothing further?
No.

I should like to help out my hon. friends from Halifax on this particular matter because I have raised it in the house on one or two occasions. I am not completely satisfied with the answer of the minister. The matter of an airport for Halifax has been in the slings for some considerable time, and I think it is pretty nearly time the department got around to doing something definite

about it. As the minister knows, the city of Halifax as such has no air facilities. There is no airport at all. If you want to get out of Halifax by air you have to cross over to Dartmouth and travel down to Eastern Passage airport which at the present time is managed and owned by the naval service. The airport at Eastern Passage is such that North Stars and other large planes cannot land there. It is a naval station and is used almost exclusively for that purpose. The city of Halifax as such has no airport whatsoever.
I think the members from that area have been patient and long-suffering because the answer we got from the minister tonight is the answer we have been getting for at least three years. He says the matter is under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think that is correct. I am sure my hon. friend does not want to make that statement. The first question I had about the Halifax airport was from my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax, and that was less than a year ago.

If you will look at the records you will find that I raised the question at least three years ago and made a detailed statement with respect to the expansion of the airport at Eastern Passage or the building of a new airport in Halifax proper.
There was no question of building it at that time.

The matter was under consideration then and the minister was going to have a look at the proposition. The minister took a look at it and a site was purchased. From the minister's answer tonight, the project is still in the embryo stage and it is all very vague. I belong to the province of Nova Scotia and I am interested in that province and in the city of Halifax from the standpoint that an airport for the city should be considered at this time as part of the national defence program. Halifax is one of the most important shipping ports east of Montreal. In the event of war it would be a very vulnerable city. It is not only very vulnerable, but if anything happened to it people would find it almost impossible to get out of the city. The members from Halifax are well aware of that.
If there was a disaster of any kind and the city had to be evacuated it certainly could not be done by highway or train. The highway is practically blocked because of the bottleneck around Fairview. Only one car at a time can get through the narrow viaduct over which the railway travels, and there would be a mess if people had to get out of

the city in a hurry. From the standpoint of civil defence the only chance of evacuating people from the city would be by air, and there is nowhere in the city a plane can land. On the other side of the harbour at Eastern Passage there are no facilities for a plane of any size to land.
I think the department should give serious consideration to the building of an airport at Halifax from the standpoint of national defence and civil defence because it is absolutely necessary for those purposes. I am not trying to browbeat the minister at all. I know he is a very co-operative minister and will do what he can, but on this matter he is not getting the co-operation behind the scenes that he should get. There are appropriations in the estimates for improvements to airports all over the country, and no section of Canada is in greater need of an airport today than the city of Halifax. I suggest that the minister should try to reach a definite understanding on the matter.
I raised the question before with the Minister of National Defence from the point of view of improving or expanding the facilities already at Eastern Passage. My understanding at that time was that it was a naval station, that they were only interested in improving it for that purpose, and that the matter of establishing a civil airport was one for the Department of Transport. As soon as the minister possibly can 1 think he should make a detailed examination of the necessity for an airport there, considering it from the point of view of civil defence and national defence, and try to give the house some definite undertaking. I know there is great anxiety in the city of Halifax on this matter, and I should like to see the minister give the house something more definite than he has been able to give so far.

Perhaps 1 was vague and indefinite in the statement I made a moment ago, but I can tell my hon. friend that a decision has been taken to establish an airport at Halifax. Before the airport is built and the strips are put in we have to get a site. The mayor of the city of Halifax came to Ottawa and assisted by the two members from that city made representations. We indicated to him that if he would make a contribution we would be glad to consider the matter. The mayor then indicated he was prepared to make a contribution and advised me of that fact. I said to him in reply that I would want to look at the site that he had in mind. Our officers have that site under consideration. They are studying it with reference to climatological conditions, and if the atmospheric conditions and the like are satisfactory after study and detailed survey 55704-1614
Supply-Transport
we will go ahead with votes in the estimates for the construction of the airport.

I understood about a year ago that consideration was being given to a new terminal building at Gander. The minister is familiar with the terminal building there. It is a converted wartime hangar. As everybody knows, Gander is one of the most important airports in Canada. Royalty are arriving there, and persons from the east. They are travelling back and forth. There is no decent terminal or hotel. 1 think consideration should be given to providing a decent terminal together with a small hotel to accommodate these people. Passengers arrive there in the hundreds every day. Has the minister anything to say on the matter? Would he give it consideration? Numerous people in Newfoundland have requested that some consideration should be given to a new terminal at Gander.
The matter is under consideration now.

As has been pointed out to the minister already, I believe, considerable concern has been expressed by the city of Charlottetown about the inadequacy of the airport there. It is used as the chief operating centre of a very progressive airline company and its runways are inadequate to such an extent that the aircraft now in use have to cut their pay loads in order to operate under the existing limitations. I understand that the city of Charlottetown is prepared to acquire and put at the disposal of the department any land which might be required in a program of extending the runways. I would be interested to know if there is provision in this item for any expansion there.
No, there is not. The mayor of the city of Charlottetown has made representations to me, and others have as well. We are sending two of our officers there to look at the airport.

Item agreed to.
517.	Contributions, subject to the approval of the governor in council, to assist municipalities in the development of and improvement to airports, the sites of which have been provided by such municipalities, $67,000.

When speaking on item 1 1 brought to the minister's attention a fact which he already knew, namely, that the people of Castlegar have asked for a grant of $50,000 in order to complete the runways of their airport. I also pointed out that the municipality of Nelson has asked for a small grant for the airstrip by the lakeshore, and the city of Revelstoke has asked for $5,000 toward the completion of their small airport. I brought to the minister's attention the great

Supply-Transport
importance of these facilities in increasing the development of the area. I notice there is no provision in the estimates for these airports. Can the minister tell the committee if further consideration has been given to these requests by his officials?
Yes. They are for the supplementary estimates.

Item agreed to.
518.	Contributions, as specified in the details of the estimates, to other governments or international agencies for the operation and maintenance of airports, air navigation and airways facilities, $275,153.
In connection with this item 518, would the minister be kind enough to explain in greater detail than is shown here the exact use to which these contributions are put?

Yes. These are contributions xhat ICAO makes on behalf of the government to Iceland; for contributions that are made to the government of Denmark, and for contributions to facilities at Grand Marais, Michigan, an airport on the transcontinental route. Roughly speaking the total is $275,000.

Item agreed to.
Administrative division-
519.	Air services administration, $235,047.
Since this is the last air item, has the minister the information concerning Sandspit?

That is the matter with reference to the crash boat? The information I have is that the departmental officials feel they could not provide a crash boat for the airport in question. If they did, it would be a provision which would have to be made for a number of other airports on our coasts that are in similar circumstances, and a policy in that regard has not been looked upon favourably, I am sorry to say.

Perhaps I had better bring another airport to the attention of the Minister of Transport. It has been taken up with the Minister of National Defence on several occasions, because it is being used and has been used for the past few years by officials of the defence department when on their way to the Wainwright military camp. At the present time there is another big military camp under construction in the lake district, and the airport is useful in that connection. It has also been suggested that should there be a bombing attack on Edmonton, and the facilities of that airport put out

of business, then Vermilion would certainly be the next airport to be used. This airport has been used by planes on their way to Lloydminster, because on a couple of occasions that airport has been flooded. The regular planes have gone on to Vermilion, and then the passengers have been taken back to Lloydminster by automobile. I should like the Minister of Transport to consult with the Minister of National Defence on this question.
I shall be glad to do so.

Quite a little money has been put into this project by the board of trade of Vermilion and the town council. The airport certainly has been of great value in the past, and should be of great value in the future if some of the things I have mentioned should take place. It would not take much money to make this an emergency landing strip of great value.
Has there been any request for or consideration given to grants to glider clubs?
There has, yes, but we have had to turn them down, because they are more of a recreational nature than anything else.
They are very useful for teaching the basic principles of flying. Other countries have made great use of gliding, and it is much cheaper than flying powered aircraft.
Yes, but on the other hand there are so many demands for air services from all parts of Canada that we feel the money could be better expended.

Item agreed to.
Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada-
521. Administration, operation and maintenance, $850,364.
This is the board of transport commissioners item, and could the minister explain the increase in that vote?
It is in part consequent upon the increase in salaries given the members of the board, which I brought down in the house earlier in the year.
But that is statutory, is it not?
The increase in salaries amounts to $53,144, and special assistance amounts to $116,000, totalling $169,144.

In the details for this special assistance, it is described as special assistance in connection with the standardization of

railway accounting procedures and1 general freight rates investigation. Does that refer to the general investigation the board is making leading to an equalization policy?
Yes, it does; and it also refers to some of the amendments which were made to the Railway Act having to do with the implementation of certain policies such as uniform accounting, and so forth.
When is it expected that they will be through with their equalization inquiry?
The last time I was able to talk to the chairman, he indicated to me that he would like to have some hearings at various places in Canada. I am not able to say when.
When will the hearings be held?
I cannot say.

Item agreed to.
Canadian Maritime Commission-
Steamship subventions for ocean services-
Pacific ocean-
524. Canada, New Zealand and Australia, service between, and if either or both the governments of Australia and of New Zealand should request or authorize the Canadian maritime commission to act on its or their behalf in contracting for this service, the Canadian maritime commission is hereby empowered so to act, $166,667.
Under this vote, could the minister tell us the present position with regard to subsidizing the Aorangi, plying between Vancouver and Australia?
The subsidy arrangement is being renewed for this year, and this is to provide for our share.

I do not know whether I am quite in order on this item, perhaps it should have been on 522; but I should like to ask the minister whether he has received any representations from the government of British Columbia or any cabinet minister, suggesting co-operation between the province and the dominion government in subsidizing the Arrow lakes steamship service?
Not in the last few months.
Is the agreement for the Australian service merely on a one year basis, or is there some longer term arrangement by which the service will be continued?
It is on a year to year basis.

Which governments are
associated?
Supply-Transport
New Zealand, Australia and Canada.
Each puts up one-third?
Canada contributes two-thirds of the subsidy.

Item agreed to.
National harbours board

525. Advances to national harbours board, subject to the provisions of section 29 of the National Harbours Board Act, to meet expenditures applicable to the calendar year 1952 on any or all of the following accounts: (a) retirement of maturing debentures-Saint John, $667,954; (b) reconstruction and capital expenditures-Halifax, $455,150; Saint John, $1,000,000; Quebec, $900,000; generally-unforeseen and miscellaneous, $100,000; less amount to be expended from replacement funds, $273,500, $2,181,650.
Have any representations been made to this government by the government of Newfoundland regarding the setting up of a national harbour board?
Yes, but not in the last seven or eight months.

The other day when the minister was speaking about local committees in the cities where there are these national harbours I think he mentioned that there was a committee in Halifax and also in Quebec. I understood from his remarks that these were committees which had been set up by interests in the cities to co-operate with the port management, and I presume to make recommendations and so on. Is that the actual picture?

In the case of Halifax, it is a corporate body that is being established by the provincial legislature. In the case of Quebec it is a group of people who have banded themselves together in an organization which is unincorporated.

Would the national harbours board and the Department of Transport cooperate if a voluntary committee were to be set up for the port of Vancouver, made up of various bodies such as the merchants' exchange, the board of trade, the Canadian Manufacturers Association and the shipping people?

Of course the national harbours board would co-operate; but the Department of Transport is not concerned with the operations of the port of Vancouver.

Supp ly-Transport
There would, of course, be no legal status for such a committee; but I should like to know whether the board would, as a matter of policy, co-operate with -a committee of that type.
If they represented a group of citizens, they would; yes.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Monday we will proceed with the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister respecting the Emergency Powers Act and the resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance respecting the Consumer Credit (Temporary Provisions) Act. Then we will move to go into supply and call only two departments. Having disposed of those matters we will take up the other three resolutions: one to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act, the second to amend the Tariff Board Act and the third to amend the Canada Elections Act. Hon. members will see that they are minor matters. Then we would take up all the finance bills, but in what order I do not know.
What are we going to do after that?
